one_liner: Pure-Go Lua 5.5 VM with an amd64/arm64 method JIT; 0.57x C Lua 5.5's time on 17 standard benchmarks, about 3x behind LuaJIT.
what_it_does: An embeddable Lua 5.5 implementation for Go programs (forked from Shopify/go-lua, largely rewritten) aimed at per-frame scripting in games, visualisers and audio tools. The Go API mirrors Lua 5.5's C API as methods on *lua.State with generic helpers (Arg[T], CheckUserData[T]), plus Go-specific extras: RegisterNumberFunction for allocation-free numeric callbacks, PushBuffer to share Go slices with Lua, Interrupt and SetAllocationLimit. lua.NewState() enables the JIT; lua.WithoutJIT() or APOGEE_JIT=off gives a plain interpreter.
how_it_is_fast: A function-at-a-time JIT with hand-written amd64 and arm64 encoders (no cgo, no LLVM) compiles functions whose pc-0 or loop-head counters pass 1000, running on the interpreter's own 16-byte stack slots with inline caches for fields, native Lua-to-Lua calls and tail calls, and exits to a Go driver for Go calls, NEWTABLE, CLOSURE and generic table access. Innermost numeric loops (and, since v1.1.2, while loops, loop nests and whole small functions) become 'kernels': typed per pc, lowered through a small IR with a linear register allocator so integers and floats live in machine registers, with constant division by Hacker's Delight magic numbers, inline sqrt/sin/cos/floor/min/max bit-exact with Go, and inlining of tiny numeric Lua functions. Separately, the redesigned value, table and call representation means numbers, booleans and calls allocate nothing.
when_to_use: Go programs that embed Lua and want it faster than C Lua on compute without cgo, e.g. per-frame game or visualiser scripts (Mandelbrot 0.20x, spectral-norm 0.33x, NBody 0.39x C Lua 5.5's time)

Numeric per-pixel or per-sample loops over Go-owned data: PushBuffer lets compiled kernels read and write a Go []float64/[]float32/[]int32/[]uint8 inline (plasma frame 0.25 ms vs 0.30 ms native Go in the bench notes)
Replacing Shopify/go-lua: about 6x less time on the standard benchmarks (geomean 5.9x C Lua's time for go-lua vs 0.57x) and no allocation per number or call
Hosts that need Lua 5.5 semantics (integer subtype, bitwise ops, <close>, global, utf8, string.pack) rather than LuaJIT's 5.1 dialect
linux or darwin on amd64 or arm64, where the JIT is enabled
when_not_to_use: Peak Lua speed with cgo allowed: LuaJIT 2.1 is about 3x faster on the same table (0.18x vs 0.57x C Lua's time), 5-15x on numeric loops such as Permute and spectral-norm, and has FFI
C or C++ hosts: it is a Go library; embed C Lua 5.5 or LuaJIT directly
Windows or other platforms: no JIT there, and the interpreter alone takes 1.8x C Lua 5.5's time

Scripts dominated by calls into Go, Go-called short Lua callbacks or table construction: on the embedding suite the JIT is slower than C Lua 5.5 on array fill and sum (1.00 vs 0.58 ms), sort with a comparator (3.84 vs 3.26 ms) and calls into Go (1.37 vs 1.07 ms)

Projects that need C modules, standard luac bytecode, an incremental Lua GC or a mature, widely used runtime: C modules cannot load, binary chunks are apogee's own format, and the project is weeks old (v1.0.0 on 2026-09-26) with 0 stars

integration.dependencies: none for the library (pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0); the bench module uses Shopify/go-lua and, with build tags, C Lua or LuaJIT via cgo
integration.platforms: JIT: linux and darwin on amd64 and arm64 (inline floor/ceil need SSE4.1 on amd64; inline sin/cos only below GOAMD64=v3); interpreter everywhere else Go runs, Windows included
integration.thread_safety: One goroutine per State; only State.Interrupt is documented as safe to call from any goroutine. Generated code cannot be preempted by Go: it spends a 65536-step budget, then returns to Go and calls runtime.Gosched so the GC can stop the world
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: runs Lua 5.5 scripts (official 5.5 test suite passes except calls.lua's binary-chunk header check), but the host API is Go mirroring the C API, C modules cannot load, binary chunks differ, only the C locale exists and collectgarbage('count') reports Go's heap

gotchas: Benchmark provenance is mislabelled: bench/README.md says the amd64 Apogee rows are from 2026-09-27 at commit 45b42e8, but PR #168 (2026-09-28) re-ran them after the five kernel-IR phases (#159-#167) and moved the geomean from 0.69x to 0.57x without changing that header; at 45b42e8 the same README showed 0.69x. Reproduce at v1.1.2 or later, not 45b42e8.

The C Lua 5.5 and LuaJIT baselines were not run under the stated 'taskset -c 0-5' pinning: the raw suite-results-amd64.txt shows every lua55 and luajit row at GOMAXPROCS 24 (no affinity mask) against 6 for every Go row, and they were measured two days earlier; on this dual-CCD 9900X3D the C rows could land on either CCD. Times are wall-clock, so Apogee's allocation-heavy rows (binary-trees, Havlak, CD) also get Go's concurrent collector on the other pinned cores while C Lua collects on the benchmark thread.

Kernels need type-stable numeric loops: math.min(x, 1) returns an integer and can knock a float loop out of its kernel (write 1.0); a kernel whose entry check keeps failing slows the ordinary loop, and while Go's write barrier is on, compiled code exits for pointer stores, native calls and kernels.

The M1 Pro table predates the Lua 5.5 port (compares with C Lua 5.4 at d5dba73) and was run on a busy machine; its Homebrew LuaJIT is anomalously slower than C Lua 5.4 on CD (329 vs 57.6 ms) and Json (19.3 vs 7.26 ms), which the project notes but does not explain.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over FakeLua (C++ Lua JIT) when the host is Go and cgo is unwanted, over Luava when you are not on the JVM, and over goja-perf or quickjs-jit when you want Lua rather than JavaScript scripting in Go with numeric code in machine registers; choose LuaJIT instead whenever cgo and Lua 5.1 are acceptable.
verified_claims_summary: On an AMD Ryzen 9 9900X3D (linux, Go 1.27.1, -ldflags=-funcalign=64, medians of 6 go test -bench runs), Apogee with its JIT took 0.57x the time of Arch Linux's C Lua 5.5.1 on the geometric mean of 14 Are We Fast Yet plus 3 Benchmarks Game programs (faster on all 17; 1.8x without the JIT; LuaJIT 2.1 0.18x), figures I recomputed exactly from the checked-in raw output; results are cross-checked by agreement tests, but the C rows are from an earlier, unpinned run.
status_note: Active (v1.1.2 released 2026-10-05, about 540 commits including go-lua history, recent ones co-authored by Claude) and MIT-licensed pure Go that installs with go get, but a few weeks old with 0 stars, so treat it as experimental.
